acts.title: The worst call of the week
text: I was working from home on Tuesday, where the ___ has never been good.
Four minutes into the call my manager told me I was ___ and asked me to repeat everything.
I said “___ me a moment” and walked into the garden, which did not help at all.
In the end she asked me to call her back on the ___, which I did not know we still had.
The call lasted forty minutes, and I am fairly sure I did not ___ any of her time usefully.
She was polite about it, which I ___ more than I said at the time.

tts: Conversation one. Hello, am I speaking to Mrs Helen Carter? — Yes, speaking. — I am calling from the Northern Energy Company, and I would like to inform you of a superb electricity deal. — Can you just stop there, please? I am not interested. I do not take sales calls. Would you remove my details from your database? Thank you. Goodbye.

Conversation two. Well, Joe, it has been great talking to you. — My pleasure. It has been good to hear all your news. — But listen, I had better get off the phone. I am still at the office and I have got a ton of work to do. — Yes, I will let you get on. Listen, before you go — do you ever see anything of Clive?

Conversation three. Sorry, Steve — just bear with me a moment. Rosie, let Thomas play with the balloon, please. Sorry about that. Yes, five hundred and fifty, did you say? Steve, look, I am going to have to go and deal with this. I am afraid you have caught me at a bad time. I will call you back in a few minutes.

Conversation four. Sorry, it is just that I cannot hear you very well. I am working from home today, and the coverage is not too good here. Sorry, Rafa, you are breaking up again. Could you just say that again? Rafa, sorry — I am losing you again. Could you call me back on my landline?

acts.title: Minority Languages in the British Isles
tts: English is now a truly global language. There are around three hundred and seventy-five million native speakers, and an incredible one and a half billion people learn it as a second, third or fourth language.
But English is not the only language native to Britain. Most of the others have their roots in Celtic culture. The Celts are thought to have arrived around 750 BCE.

Today around sixty thousand people speak Scottish Gaelic, most of them in the Highlands or on the islands off the north-western coast. Thanks to emigration in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, Scottish Gaelic communities have developed in Canada too.

The closest language to Scottish Gaelic is Irish. It is the first official language of the Republic, and while there are only around eighty thousand native speakers, almost everybody has some knowledge of it.
In Wales, around five hundred and sixty thousand people speak Welsh — almost twenty per cent of the population.

Cornish is similar to Welsh, but far fewer people speak it. The last native speaker died over two hundred and forty years ago, and the language was declared extinct in the nineteenth century. In recent years it has made a comeback: today around three to five hundred people speak it fluently.
Experts predict that around fifty per cent of the world’s six thousand five hundred languages could be extinct by the end of the century.

acts.title: Getting off the phone, and getting through a bad line
rule: Phone English is a small, fixed set of phrases. Almost none of it is improvised, which is why it can be learnt in one lesson and why sounding wrong on the phone is so noticeable. The two hardest jobs are ending a call the other person wants to continue, and admitting you cannot hear.
points: Signal first, then give a reason, then close. Three moves, always in that order.
Bear with me is the standard phrase. A moment or for a moment both work; what is fixed is the with.
You are breaking up describes the other person; the coverage isn’t good here describes you.
I’m afraid… turns a refusal into an apology, and is almost obligatory with a stranger.
eg: It’s been great talking to you.
Signals the end without saying goodbye yet.
I’d better get off the phone — I’ve got a ton of work to do.
Signal plus reason.
I’ll let you get on.
Puts the reason on the other person. Very polite.
I won’t take up any more of your time.
The most formal of the three closings.
Just bear with me a moment.
The with is compulsory. Never “bear me a moment”.
I’m afraid you’ve caught me at a bad time.
A refusal with the apology built in.
Sorry, you’re breaking up.
Their signal is failing.
The coverage isn’t too good here.
Your signal is failing.
Could you call me back on my landline?
A request, so could, not can.
I don’t take sales calls.
Present simple for a standing policy — flat, and deliberately final.
acts.careful: “Can you bear me a moment?” and “I’ll let you get on with” are both wrong. These phrases are fixed: bear with me, let you get on.

write.q: Write an informal email of about 150 words to a friend you have not spoken to for a long time, giving your news. Use the present perfect continuous at least twice for what you have been doing, the present perfect simple at least twice for what you have finished, and end by suggesting a time to catch up.
plan: why you have not been in touch
write.model:
Hi Aidana,

It seems like ages since we were in touch, and it is entirely my fault — I have been meaning to write since about March.

Work has been the reason. We have been rebuilding the whole reporting system since the spring, which has taken roughly three times as long as anybody promised. The good news is that we have finally finished the first stage, and I have been sleeping properly again for about a fortnight.

The other news is better. My sister has had twins. She is over the moon and slightly grey, and I have been round there most weekends learning how to hold two babies at once.

How have you been? I have heard almost nothing since you moved. Let us catch up properly — are you free on a Sunday this month?

Tilek
